description: Absolute and relative poverty, the underclass, the cycle of deprivation and social exclusion.
content_html:
Defining Poverty

Poverty is not simply a matter of having less money than others. Sociologists distinguish between different definitions of poverty, and these choices have significant consequences for how many people are counted as poor and what solutions are proposed. Two key distinctions are between absolute poverty and relative poverty. These definitions reflect competing perspectives on what poverty means and how it should be measured.

Key Fact

Townsend (1979) argued that relative deprivation is the most meaningful measure of poverty because it accounts for social participation, not just physical survival. Murray (1984) focused on the “underclass” — a cultural explanation rooted in the New Right tradition. These two perspectives offer fundamentally different diagnoses of, and prescriptions for, poverty.

Absolute and Relative Poverty

Absolute poverty refers to a condition in which an individual lacks the bare minimum needed to survive physically — adequate food, shelter and clothing. It is usually defined by a fixed threshold that does not change as society becomes wealthier. While absolute poverty in this extreme sense is rare in the contemporary UK due to the welfare state, it remains a serious issue globally and has been associated with homelessness and destitution in the UK context, particularly during periods of welfare cuts.

Relative poverty, by contrast, is defined in relation to the living standards prevailing in a given society at a particular time. A household living in relative poverty may have enough food to survive but lacks the resources to participate in social and cultural activities considered normal by the majority. Common UK thresholds measure relative poverty as income below 60% of median household income. Relative poverty is sensitive to inequality — if society becomes wealthier overall but the gap between rich and poor widens, relative poverty can increase even if absolute living standards improve for the poor.

A common misconception is to treat “poverty” as a single concept. The spec requires students to distinguish absolute from relative poverty precisely because they lead to very different conclusions about how serious poverty is and what should be done about it. Absolute poverty focuses on physical survival; relative poverty focuses on social participation. Townsend explicitly argued that relative deprivation is the more sociologically meaningful concept because poverty is always experienced in a social and cultural context, not in biological isolation. Students should be careful not to conflate the two in a 2-mark Define answer — each definition earns a separate mark.

Townsend: Relative Deprivation and the Deprivation Index

Peter Townsend’s major study Poverty in the United Kingdom (1979) is one of the most influential sociological investigations of poverty. Townsend argued that previous measures of poverty were inadequate because they used arbitrary income thresholds that failed to capture the lived experience of deprivation. His preferred measure was relative deprivation. He devised a deprivation index that scored households on a wide range of variables — not just income but diet, fuel, clothing, housing, health, education and social activities. Using this index on a sample of over 2,000 households, Townsend concluded that over 22% of the UK population was living in poverty in 1968–69, far higher than the government’s own poverty standard of approximately 6%. Townsend’s method captured the extent to which poverty excluded people from the social life of their community: being unable to afford a child’s birthday party or a meal with friends were counted as dimensions of deprivation alongside material lack.

Charles Murray, writing from a New Right perspective, offered a very different account. In Losing Ground (1984), Murray argued that the growth of welfare benefits had created a growing underclass. Government welfare policies had, in Murray’s view, undermined self-sufficiency by making it rational for individuals — especially single parents and young unemployed people — to depend on benefits rather than seek paid work.

Murray visited Britain in the late 1980s and argued the UK was developing a similar underclass, characterised by rising rates of lone parenthood, rising crime and an apparent unwillingness among some young people to seek employment. Murray identified a dependency culture — a set of values and habits that normalised benefit receipt and undermined the traditional values of work, family and self-reliance. Murray’s argument has attracted severe criticism. Critics point out that his evidence base was weak, and that research consistently shows most people on benefits hold conventional values and aspire to employment. Townsend’s structural approach suggests poverty results from material deprivation and social exclusion — external conditions that shape behaviour — not from a cultural pathology of the poor themselves. Feminist critics note that Murray’s focus on lone-parent families (predominantly headed by women) implicitly blames women for poverty, ignoring structural causes including the gender pay gap and domestic responsibilities.

Cycle of Deprivation, Social Exclusion and Inclusion

The cycle of deprivation describes how poverty can be self-reinforcing across generations. Children raised in poverty face disadvantages in nutrition, housing quality, educational resources and aspirations that reduce their chances of escaping poverty as adults. Poor health in childhood may limit educational attainment; limited educational attainment restricts employment prospects; limited employment income creates material deprivation for the next generation. Sociologists who take a structural view of poverty regard the cycle of deprivation as evidence that poverty is a systemic condition, not an individual failing — intervention must be at the structural level to break the cycle.

Social exclusion is a broader concept that captures how poverty operates across multiple dimensions simultaneously. An individual experiencing social exclusion may lack not only income but employment, decent housing, access to health services, educational opportunity and social participation. Social inclusion policies attempt to address this multi-dimensional disadvantage by providing access to services, employment support and community participation alongside income support.

Groups Prone to Poverty: Lone Parents, the Elderly, Ethnic Minorities

Poverty is not evenly distributed. Sociologists identify specific groups who are disproportionately likely to experience poverty. Lone parents — predominantly women — face high poverty risk because they combine responsibility for childcare with dependence on a single income, often from part-time or lower-paid employment. The gender pay gap and the cost of childcare compound this disadvantage. Elderly people on fixed or state pensions are vulnerable to poverty when living costs rise, and women are particularly at risk because career breaks and part-time work reduce pension accumulation. Ethnic minorities face higher poverty rates linked to employment discrimination, lower average wages and concentration in areas with fewer economic opportunities.

Globalisation and Poverty

Globalisation has affected poverty patterns in the UK. The movement of manufacturing jobs to lower-wage economies — the relocation of car, steel and textile production to South and East Asia from the 1980s onwards — reduced the availability of stable manual employment in many UK communities, increasing unemployment and economic insecurity among working-class populations. The shift to a service economy has created some new employment but often in lower-paid or less secure conditions. Marxists argue this reflects the fundamental dynamic of capitalism: the tendency to concentrate wealth at the top while insecurity grows among the proletariat. Globalisation has increased wealth at the top end, potentially widening the gap between the richest and poorest and increasing relative poverty even as absolute living standards improve for some.

Key Fact

In a 12-mark Evaluate question on poverty, always present Murray’s New Right underclass thesis as “Murray’s argument that…” rather than as fact — it is contested. Balance it with Townsend’s structural relative deprivation approach and at least one other perspective (Marxist: poverty as product of class exploitation and globalisation; feminist: poverty disproportionately affects women due to patriarchal structures in employment and domestic life).
exam_tip_html: On a 2-mark Define question asking you to define “relative poverty,” do not simply write “when people don’t have much money.” The mark scheme expects a sociological definition: relative poverty is the condition of lacking resources needed to participate in the standard of living considered normal in a given society — reference to society’s standards is the second mark. For the 12-mark Evaluate, students often give only Townsend or only Murray. The highest marks come from presenting both perspectives and evaluating them against each other: Townsend’s deprivation index as a structural measurement tool versus Murray’s cultural dependency culture thesis. Then add a Marxist or feminist dimension and close with a supported judgement about which explanation best accounts for poverty in contemporary Britain.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Absolute poverty describes a lack of resources for basic physical survival; relative poverty describes a lack of resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in society. Townsend's deprivation index found over 22% of the UK population in poverty in 1968-69, far above official estimates, using a relative approach that measured social participation.
  • Murray's New Right underclass thesis attributes poverty to a dependency culture created by welfare benefits, focusing on cultural rather than structural causes. This view is widely contested: critics argue it victim-blames the poor, particularly lone mothers, and lacks strong evidence. The cycle of deprivation and social exclusion frameworks offer structural alternatives.
  • Globalisation has increased labour market insecurity in the UK by relocating manufacturing employment, widening relative poverty even as absolute living standards improve. Poverty disproportionately affects lone parents (predominantly women), the elderly and some ethnic minority groups.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'relative poverty'?
A) Lacking enough food to survive physically
B) Earning less than the national average wage
C) Lacking resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in society
D) Having no access to state welfare benefits
practice_questions.marks: C) Lacking resources to participate in the standard of living considered normal in society [1 mark]

1 mark for identifying that absolute poverty refers to a lack of basic necessities; 1 mark for specifying what those necessities are or explaining that the threshold is fixed (e.g. 'Absolute poverty is a condition in which an individual lacks the minimum resources required for physical survival, such as adequate food, shelter and clothing, measured against a fixed threshold that does not vary with overall living standards in society.').

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe Townsend's concept of the 'cycle of deprivation'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the cycle of deprivation as the intergenerational reproduction of poverty. 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'The cycle of deprivation describes how poverty can be self-reinforcing across generations. Children raised in poverty face interconnected disadvantages — in nutrition, housing quality, educational resources and aspirations — that reduce their chances of escaping poverty as adults. Limited educational attainment restricts employment prospects; limited income creates material deprivation for the next generation. Structural interventions at the level of income, housing and education are therefore needed to break the cycle, rather than focusing on individual behaviour.'

practice_questions.text: Describe Murray's New Right explanation of poverty, including the concept of the underclass.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Murray argued that welfare benefits created a growing underclass dependent on state support rather than employment (1 mark); he identified a dependency culture — a set of values normalising benefit receipt and undermining work and family responsibility (1 mark); he identified rising lone parenthood, crime and youth unemployment as signs of underclass growth (1 mark); critics argue Murray's evidence is weak, that most benefit recipients hold conventional values and aspire to employment, and that his analysis ignores structural causes including the gender pay gap and globalisation (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that poverty in modern Britain is best explained by the behaviour and attitudes of poor people themselves.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two perspectives developed in detail, both sides, sustained vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Murray's New Right underclass and dependency culture thesis explained in depth — welfare dependency, rising lone parenthood, unwillingness to seek employment. Contrasting: Townsend's structural relative deprivation approach (poverty as lack of resources for social participation, deprivation index, 22%); Marxist explanation (structural class exploitation, globalisation increasing labour insecurity); feminist critique of Murray (victim-blames lone mothers, ignores gender pay gap and domestic responsibilities). Named sociologists throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both cultural and structural sides present; named sociologists; judgement offered.

Developing: Mostly one side; some vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description; few named theorists; little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate sociological explanations of poverty in contemporary British society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Cultural explanation (Murray's underclass, dependency culture) explained and evaluated with evidence against it. Structural explanations developed in depth: Townsend's relative deprivation and deprivation index (22% finding, social participation measure); Marxist explanation (class exploitation, surplus value extraction, globalisation relocating manufacturing and increasing insecurity); feminist critique (poverty disproportionately affects women — lone parents, elderly women on low pensions — linked to gender pay gap and domestic responsibilities — Walby's structures of patriarchy). Cycle of deprivation and social exclusion as structural frameworks. Groups prone to poverty identified (lone parents, elderly, ethnic minorities). Supported judgement weighing cultural versus structural explanations, noting the evidence strongly supports structural accounts.

Secure: Most arguments present; Townsend and Murray both developed; contrasting perspectives used; judgement offered.

Developing: Mostly Townsend or Murray without sufficient evaluation of the other; weak comparative structure; assertive conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of poverty types; few named theorists; little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is Townsend's preferred measure of poverty?
options: Relative income compared with average wages

knowledge_checks.q: Murray's New Right theory argues that welfare benefits create a 'dependency _____' that discourages self-sufficiency.
Poverty defined as lacking the resources to participate in activities considered normal in society is called _____ poverty.
Townsend's tool for measuring poverty across a range of indicators including diet, housing and social activities was called a _____ index.
Match each sociologist to their key concept about poverty:
right: Relative deprivation — poverty measured by social participation, not just income; found 22% of UK in poverty
Underclass — poverty caused by welfare dependency and a dependency culture normalising benefit receipt
Poverty as the product of class exploitation — the bourgeoisie extract surplus value, keeping wages low

flashcard_questions.a: Lacking the basic resources necessary for physical survival, such as adequate food, shelter and clothing.
Lacking resources needed to participate in the standard of living considered normal in a given society.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Townsend's concept of relative deprivation?
flashcard_questions.a: Poverty defined as lacking resources to participate in activities and living conditions normal in society — not just about income.
A measurement tool scoring households on diet, housing, health, education and social activities to assess poverty more broadly than income alone.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of the UK population did Townsend find was living in poverty using his deprivation index?
flashcard_questions.a: Over 22% — far higher than the government's own estimate of around 6%.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Murray's concept of the underclass?
flashcard_questions.a: A group at the bottom of society characterised by long-term welfare dependency, high crime rates and disconnection from work and family values.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a dependency culture in Murray's New Right theory?
flashcard_questions.a: A value system normalising welfare benefit receipt, undermining work, family responsibility and self-reliance.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the cycle of deprivation?
flashcard_questions.a: The intergenerational transmission of disadvantage — children raised in poverty face barriers that make it more likely they will be poor as adults.
The process by which individuals are prevented from full participation in economic, social, political and cultural life as a result of poverty and related disadvantages.

flashcard_questions.q: How does globalisation affect poverty in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: It increases labour market insecurity by relocating manufacturing jobs abroad, potentially widening relative poverty even as absolute standards rise.

flashcard_questions.q: How do feminist sociologists criticise Murray's underclass thesis?
flashcard_questions.a: It victim-blames lone mothers (mostly women) while ignoring structural causes such as the gender pay gap and domestic responsibilities.

flashcard_questions.q: Name three groups identified as disproportionately likely to experience poverty in the UK.
flashcard_questions.a: Lone parents (predominantly women), elderly people on fixed pensions, and some ethnic minority groups facing employment discrimination.

glossary_terms.definition: A condition in which individuals lack the resources necessary for basic physical survival, such as food, shelter and clothing.
A condition in which individuals lack the resources needed to participate fully in the standard of living considered normal in their society.
Townsend's concept of poverty defined as lacking the resources to participate in activities and living conditions considered normal in a given society.
Townsend's tool for measuring poverty by scoring households on a range of variables including diet, fuel, clothing, housing, health, education and social activities.
In Murray's New Right theory, a group at the bottom of society characterised by long-term welfare dependency, high crime rates and disconnection from mainstream work and family values.
Murray's New Right concept of a value system in which welfare dependency is normalised, undermining work, family responsibility and self-reliance.
The intergenerational transmission of disadvantage, in which children raised in poverty are more likely to experience poverty as adults because of the interconnected barriers it creates.
The process by which individuals or groups are prevented from full participation in economic, social, political and cultural life as a result of poverty and related disadvantages.
